## How to read this lecture

[Last time](../general-relativity/index.qmd) we established that gravity is
geometry, and looked at the places where that shows up as a small correction to
a nearly flat spacetime: an orbit that fails to close by 43 arcseconds a
century, a star that shifts by under two arcseconds during an eclipse.

This lecture is what happens when the correction stops being small. Everything
here follows from the same curvature, pushed until it dominates: light that
climbs out of a well and arrives reddened, clocks that run at half speed,
a surface from which nothing returns at all, and the ripples that two merging
black holes send across the universe.

There is one number to carry through all of it. Every result below is written
in terms of how close you are to a mass **in units of its Schwarzschild
radius** — and once you are working in those units, the mass itself usually
cancels out. That is not an accident of algebra. It is the statement that
strong gravity looks the same around a stellar-mass black hole and around a
supermassive one; only the scale changes.

### The readings

* **Kutner sections 8.3.3, 8.3.4 and 8.4.** This is the main reading and it
  tracks these notes closely — gravitational redshift, gravitational radiation,
  and black holes, in that order.
* Einstein Online, [Gravitational redshift and White Dwarf
  stars](https://www.einstein-online.info/en/spotlight/redshift_white_dwarfs/) —
  the effect measured on a real star, which is a useful corrective to how
  abstract it can feel.
* Einstein Online, [Spacetime
  singularities](https://www.einstein-online.info/en/spotlight/singularities/)
  and [The Singularity
  Theorem](https://www.einstein-online.info/en/spotlight/the-singularity-theorem/),
  on what it means for a theory to predict its own breakdown. The second one is
  about the work that won the 2020 Nobel Prize.

**If you want a different picture of curvature**, ScienceClic's [A new way to
visualize General Relativity](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wrwgIjBUYVc)
builds the whole thing without ever drawing a rubber sheet. Given
[what we said about that analogy last time](../general-relativity/index.qmd),
it is worth twenty minutes. Optional.

## Black holes, from the theory this time

You already derived the Schwarzschild radius in
[lecture 1](../scales-and-schwarzschild/index.qmd), using an argument about
escape velocity: set the escape speed equal to $c$ and solve for the radius.
That argument gives the right answer,

$$
r_S = \frac{2 G M}{c^2} \approx 3\ \mathrm{km}\left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right),
$$ {#eq-rs-again}

and it is a good way to remember the formula. But it is not really a derivation,
because it treats light as a slow-moving cannonball that gravity pulls back.
Now you have the real reason. Spacetime near a sufficiently compact mass is
curved so steeply that all paths leading outward from inside a certain surface
instead lead inward. Nothing gets out because there is no "out" to go to.

The metric describing spacetime around a non-spinning mass $M$ is the
**Schwarzschild metric**, and the single feature worth carrying away is what
happens to it at large distance: for $r \gg r_S$ it reduces to the flat
spacetime of special relativity. Curvature is a local business. Far from the
mass, Einstein's picture and Newton's agree, which is why nobody noticed for two
hundred years.

One new radius is worth knowing. At $1.5\,r_S$ there is a **photon sphere**,
where gravity is strong enough that light itself can orbit. A photon aimed just
right there circles the black hole indefinitely. It is an unstable orbit — the
slightest nudge sends the photon in or out — but it is the reason a black hole
casts the particular shadow that the Event Horizon Telescope images show.

:::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Work out the Schwarzschild radius of a person"}
Take a 70 kg person and ask what radius they would need to be compressed to in
order to become a black hole. Using @eq-rs-again, first in solar masses:

$$
M = 70\ \mathrm{kg} \times \frac{10^{3}\ \mathrm{g}}{1\ \mathrm{kg}}
    \times \frac{1\ M_\odot}{1.989 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}
  = 3.5 \times 10^{-29}\ M_\odot .
$$

Then

$$
r_S = 3\ \mathrm{km} \times 3.5 \times 10^{-29}
    = 1.0 \times 10^{-28}\ \mathrm{km}
    \times \frac{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}
    = 1.0 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm}.
$$

For comparison, an atomic nucleus is about $10^{-13}\ \mathrm{cm}$ across. Your
personal Schwarzschild radius is ten orders of magnitude smaller than a nucleus.
This is why you are not a black hole, and it is a good reminder of how
absurdly compact a stellar-mass black hole is.
::::

### Curvature as a number

So far "curvature" has been a word. Here is how to put a number on it.

The quantity that matters is the ratio

$$
\text{curvature} = \frac{r_S}{R},
$$ {#eq-curvature}

where $R$ is how far you are from the center of an object of mass $M$, and
$r_S$ is that object's Schwarzschild radius from @eq-rs-again. It is a pure
number — a length over a length — and it measures **the strength of the
gravitational field** in the only way general relativity really cares about:
how close you are to being a black hole.

Read the extremes off it directly. At the event horizon $R = r_S$, so the
curvature is exactly 1 — the maximum. Far away, $r_S/R \to 0$ and spacetime is
flat, which is why Newton worked for two hundred years. Everything interesting
happens between those.

The useful thing about @eq-curvature is that it lets you compare situations that
otherwise have nothing in common. A stellar-mass black hole, the surface of the
Sun and a planetary orbit are wildly different objects, but each has a value of
$r_S/R$, and that single number tells you how much of a correction general
relativity is going to make. You will work three of them in class.

### Where the theory runs out

One more thing about the picture, and it is not a quibble about analogies.

Follow the Schwarzschild solution inward and it does not stop at the horizon.
At the center it predicts a point of **infinite density** — a singularity. That
is not a description of something that exists. Infinite density is what a theory
says when it has been pushed past its own domain of validity, in the same way
that Newtonian gravity "predicts" infinite escape velocity at zero radius.

So the singularity is best read as **general relativity announcing its own
limit.** Something else takes over before you get there, and the something else
has to reconcile gravity with quantum mechanics — a theory of quantum gravity
that does not yet exist. The horizon is real physics. The singularity is a
signpost saying the theory ends here.


::::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-blackholes}

**Exercise 5.1.** The Schwarzschild radius of the Sun is about
$3\ \mathrm{km}$. Does that mean the innermost $3\ \mathrm{km}$ of the Sun is a
black hole? Explain.

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**No**, and the reason is worth being precise about.

@eq-rs-again takes the mass $M$ of the object and returns a radius. When you put
in a whole solar mass you get $3\ \mathrm{km}$, and what that tells you is: *if
you compressed the entire Sun inside a 3 km sphere, it would be a black hole.*
The Sun is not compressed like that — its mass is spread over $7\times10^{5}$
km — so nothing about the real Sun is inside its own Schwarzschild radius.

Now ask about the innermost 3 km specifically. That region contains only the
mass actually inside it. At the Sun's central density of roughly
$150\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, that is about $10^{19}\ \mathrm{g}$ — around
$10^{-14}\,M_\odot$ — and *that* mass has a Schwarzschild radius of about
$10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Which is smaller than an atom, and about twelve orders
of magnitude short of the 3 km it would need to fill.

**The general trap:** $r_S$ is computed from the mass you enclose, so quoting an
object's Schwarzschild radius says nothing about any sub-region of it.
::::

**Exercise 5.2.** Is there anywhere near a black hole where you could look
straight ahead and see the back of your own head? Explain.

:::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Ask what would have to be true of a light ray that leaves the back of your head
and arrives at your eyes from in front. It has to go all the way around.

There is exactly one radius where light does that, and the lecture names it.
::::

**Exercise 5.3.** A black hole's "average density" can be defined as its mass
divided by the volume of a sphere of radius $r_S$. For what mass is that
density equal to $1\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, the density of water?

*Before you calculate: guess whether the answer is a small black hole or a big
one, and why.*

## Gravitational redshift

A photon climbing out of a gravitational well arrives with less energy than it
started with. Since a photon's energy is $E = h\nu = hc/\lambda$, losing energy
means a longer wavelength: the light is **redshifted**.

:::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Decide what speed the escaping light has when it reaches you"}
Exactly $c$. Not less.

This trips people up every year, because "the photon loses energy climbing out"
sounds like it should slow down, the way a thrown ball does. But light does not
work that way — its speed in vacuum is $c$ for every observer, which is the
foundation everything in [lecture 3](../special-relativity/index.qmd) was built
on, and general relativity does not overturn it.

The energy has to go somewhere, so it comes out of the *frequency* instead. The
photon arrives at the same speed, redder.
::::

Here is an approximate derivation. It is not rigorous — it treats the photon as
though it had a mass, which it does not — but it gets remarkably close and shows
where the effect comes from.

Use conservation of energy between the emission point at radius $r$ and infinity,
where there is no gravity. Assign the photon a "gravitational mass" $m$ through
$E = hc/\lambda_0 = mc^2$, so that $m = h/\lambda_0 c$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{hc}{\lambda} &= \frac{hc}{\lambda_0} - \frac{GMm}{r} \\[0.8em]
\frac{1}{\lambda} &= \frac{1}{\lambda_0} - \frac{GM}{r}\cdot\frac{m}{hc} \\[0.8em]
\frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda} &= 1 - \frac{GM}{r}
   \left(\frac{h}{\lambda_0 c}\right)\left(\frac{\lambda_0}{hc}\right)
 = 1 - \frac{GM}{r c^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-redshift-approx}

The full treatment in general relativity gives something very close, with a
square root and a factor of two:

$$
\lambda = \frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{2GM}{r c^2}}}
        = \frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{r_S}{r}}}.
$$ {#eq-redshift}

@eq-redshift is the one to use. Written in terms of $r_S$ it is easy to read:
the redshift depends only on how close you are to the horizon *in units of the
Schwarzschild radius*.

And look at what it does as $r \to r_S$. The square root goes to zero and
$\lambda \to \infty$. **A photon emitted exactly at the Schwarzschild radius
arrives at infinite wavelength and zero energy** — which is to say, it never
arrives at all. That is the event horizon, derived a second way.

### A test at the Galactic center

The effect has been measured on the star S0-2, the same star whose orbital
precession you met [last time](../general-relativity/index.qmd). At closest
approach it passes within about 120 astronomical units of Sgr A\*, a
$4\times10^{6}\,M_\odot$ black hole — close enough that the light we receive
from it is measurably reddened, on top of the ordinary Doppler shift from its
motion.

Separating the two is the hard part of the measurement and the reason it took
decades of monitoring: you have to know the orbit well enough to predict the
Doppler shift exactly, and then show that what is left over is the
gravitational piece. It is the same star doing double duty as a test of general
relativity, in two independent ways.

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-redshift}

**Exercise 5.4.** A neutron star has mass $M = 1.4\,M_\odot$ and radius
$R = 10\ \mathrm{km}$. An atomic transition on its surface emits light at a rest
wavelength of $486.1\ \mathrm{nm}$.

(a) Compute the redshift $z = \Delta\lambda/\lambda_0$ of light escaping from
    the surface to a distant observer.
(b) What wavelength does the distant observer measure?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(a)** First get the Schwarzschild radius, carrying the units through:

$$
r_S = \frac{2GM}{c^2}
    = \frac{2\,(6.674\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}})
            (1.4)(1.989\times10^{33}\ \mathrm{g})}
           {(2.998\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}})^2}.
$$

Cancel the units before touching the numbers:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \cdot \mathrm{g}}
     {\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-2}}}
 = \frac{\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-2}}}
 = \mathrm{cm}.
$$

*Do the units make sense?* Centimeters are a length, and a radius is a length,
so yes. Now the arithmetic:

$$
r_S = 4.14 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}
    \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{km}}{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}
    = 4.14\ \mathrm{km}.
$$

So $r_S/R = 4.14/10 = 0.414$, a pure number. From @eq-redshift,

$$
\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.414}} = \frac{1}{0.766} = 1.306,
$$

so $z = \lambda/\lambda_0 - 1 = \boxed{0.31}$.

**(b)** $\lambda = 1.306 \times 486.1\ \mathrm{nm} = \boxed{635\ \mathrm{nm}}$.

Worth noticing: 486.1 nm is the blue-green H$\beta$ line, and 635 nm is
distinctly red. A 31% redshift is not subtle — this is an effect you could see
by eye.
::::

**Exercise 5.5.** Two astronauts park $60\ \mathrm{km}$ from a
$10\,M_\odot$ black hole and shine a $400\ \mathrm{nm}$ laser back toward Earth,
which is effectively infinitely far away. What wavelength do we measure?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
Work in units of $r_S$ — you do not need the black hole's mass in grams for
anything except getting $r_S$ itself, and @eq-rs-again gives you that in one
step.

The answer is $561\ \mathrm{nm}$. The laser leaves violet and arrives
yellow-green.
::::

**Exercise 5.6.** At what radius, in units of $r_S$, must a photon be emitted so
that a distant observer measures its wavelength to be exactly **twice** the
emitted wavelength?

*(No hints on this one. The algebra is three lines, and the answer is a clean
multiple of $r_S$.)*

**Exercise 5.7.** A white dwarf has mass $1\,M_\odot$ and radius
$5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{km}$. The H$\alpha$ line has a rest wavelength of
$656.3\ \mathrm{nm}$. To what wavelength is it shifted by the time a distant
observer sees it?

*How many significant figures do you need to carry to see the effect at all?
That is part of the question.*

## Gravitational time dilation

The same factor that stretches wavelengths stretches time. This is not a
coincidence — a wave's frequency *is* a clock, so anything that lowers the
frequency of arriving light is also slowing the rate at which the emitter's
seconds reach you.

**All processes run slower in the presence of gravity**, and the deeper into the
well, the slower they run. A clock at radius $r$ ticks slowly compared to a
clock far away by the factor

$$
\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta t} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{r_S}{r}},
$$ {#eq-timedilation-gr}

which is exactly the square root from @eq-redshift.

:::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Decide which runs slowest: a clock in Ann Arbor, in Denver, or in Miami"}
**Miami.** The rule is that deeper in the gravitational well means slower, and
"deeper" means lower — closer to the center of the Earth. Miami is at sea level,
Ann Arbor is about 880 feet up, and Denver is a mile up.

So the order from slowest to fastest is Miami, then Ann Arbor, then Denver. The
mile-high city gets the fastest clocks of the three.

The effect is real and routinely measured, but it is tiny at these depths —
parts in $10^{16}$. It matters enormously for GPS satellites, whose clocks are
corrected for it, and it becomes overwhelming near a black hole, which is where
we are going next.
::::

Now push @eq-timedilation-gr to its limit. As $r \to r_S$, the square root goes
to zero and a distant observer sees the infalling clock tick more and more
slowly, approaching a stop. **From far away, an object takes infinite time to
reach the event horizon.** It appears to freeze there, fading and reddening as
it goes, and never quite arrives.

But the object itself experiences nothing of the sort. An observer riding along
with the infalling matter crosses the horizon in a perfectly finite time, notices
nothing locally remarkable about the crossing, and continues inward to the
center. Both accounts are correct. They are different observers' descriptions
of the same events, which should feel familiar after
[lecture 3](../special-relativity/index.qmd) — except that here the disagreement
is produced by curvature rather than relative motion.

@fig-infall shows both accounts side by side, for a particle spiraling into a
black hole. The two panels are the *same* infall, clocked two different ways.

![The same infalling particle, timed two ways. The left panel advances by the
particle's own **proper time** $t_p$, and the particle spirals in and crosses
the horizon after a finite amount of it. The right panel advances by the

particle never gets there — it winds around and around, frozen against the
horizon. Neither panel is wrong. Note that this is a *rotating* black hole, so

width="100%"

### Why acceleration breaks the symmetry

Where does @eq-timedilation-gr come from? Here is the argument, and it starts
somewhere that looks unrelated.

Put yourself in a rocket, accelerating. Jackie is with you, at the back; you are
at the front. You each hold a lightbulb that flashes according to your own local
clock, and at rest — or at any constant velocity — the two flash at the same
rate. Nothing distinguishes you.

Now switch the engines on. The bulbs no longer agree: **the one at the back of
the ship flashes more slowly**, and you both see it. Think about why. The ship
is speeding up the whole time a flash is in transit, so light traveling forward
from Jackie to you is chasing a receiver that keeps getting faster — the flashes
arrive stretched out. Light traveling backward from you to Jackie meets a
receiver rushing to intercept it, and arrives bunched up.

**And crucially, you and Jackie agree about which clock is slow.** That is what
makes this different from
[special relativity](../special-relativity/index.qmd), where each of two
inertial observers sees the other's clock running slow and neither is wrong.
Acceleration breaks the symmetry. There is now a fact of the matter about who is
behind.

Now apply the equivalence principle, which says you cannot tell constant
acceleration from a uniform gravitational field. If the clock at the back of an
accelerating ship runs slow, then **a clock deeper in a gravitational well runs
slow**, full stop — and everyone agrees it does. The "back of the ship" and
"deeper in the well" are the same situation wearing different clothes.

How much slower depends on how deep, and @eq-curvature is how we measure
that. Carrying the argument through properly gives @eq-timedilation-gr,

$$
\Delta\tau = \Delta t\sqrt{1 - \frac{r_S}{R}},
$$ {#eq-timedilation-ship}

where $\Delta\tau$ is the time that elapses in the gravitational field and
$\Delta t$ is the time that elapses for an observer far away, where spacetime is
flat.

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-timedilation}

**Exercise 5.8.** How does the rate of a clock at $1.5\,r_S$ from a
$3\,M_\odot$ black hole compare with the rate of a clock far away?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
Everything in @eq-timedilation-gr depends on $r$ only through $r_S/r$, and you
are handed $r$ in units of $r_S$ already. **You never need the mass** — the
$3\,M_\odot$ is there to see whether you reach for it.

The clock runs at $\sqrt{1-1/1.5} = 0.577$, about **58%** of the distant rate.
::::

**Exercise 5.9.** In a hypothetical movie, two astronauts go close to a black
hole. One hour passes for them; ten hours pass on Earth, effectively infinitely
far away. How close to the black hole did they get, in units of $r_S$?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
You are given the *ratio* of elapsed times, which is exactly the factor
in @eq-timedilation-gr. You never need the black hole's mass — the answer
is in units of $r_S$ and the mass cancels out.

The answer is $r = 1.01\,r_S$. Which is worth pausing on: to get a factor of ten,
they had to be within one percent of the horizon.
::::

**Exercise 5.10.** Explain, in three or four sentences, how it can be true both
that a distant observer never sees an object cross the event horizon *and* that
the object crosses it in finite time by its own clock. Your answer should not
require one of the two observers to be mistaken.

*(No solution given. This is the conceptual heart of the section, and it is
exactly the kind of thing worth being able to say out loud.)*

## Gravitational waves

If mass-energy curves spacetime, then mass-energy that *moves* should make the
curvature change — and a changing curvature should propagate. General relativity
predicts exactly that: **ripples in the curvature of spacetime**, traveling at
$c$, in close analogy to light waves being ripples in the electromagnetic field.

A passing gravitational wave stretches space one way and squeezes it the other,
alternating. Drop a ring of free particles in the path of one and the ring
distorts to an ellipse, then to an ellipse the other way, then back.

The quantity that describes the size of the effect is the **strain**,

$$
h = \frac{\Delta x}{x},
$$ {#eq-strain}

the fractional change in the distance between two points. It is a pure number,
and it is very, very small.

### LIGO

The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory measures that strain
directly. A laser beam is split and sent down two perpendicular 4 km arms,
bounced back and forth about 280 times by mirrors so that the effective path is
around 1120 km, then recombined at a detector. The arms are arranged so the two
beams cancel exactly when nothing is happening. A passing wave changes the
lengths of the two arms by different amounts, the cancellation stops being
perfect, and a signal appears.

The sensitivity this achieves is difficult to overstate: LIGO can detect a change
in arm length of about **one thousandth the size of a proton**.

![LIGO Hanford, in eastern Washington. The two arms run away from the corner
station at right angles, each four kilometers long, and the beam tubes are held
under vacuum along their whole length. There is an identical installation at
Livingston, Louisiana, three thousand kilometers away — and it takes both of
them to claim a detection. Photograph by the LIGO Laboratory; public
domain.](ligo-hanford-aerial.jpg){#fig-ligo
width="100%"
fig-alt="Aerial photograph of a low white building complex in flat, dry
scrubland. Two long straight enclosed tubes leave the building at right angles
to each other and run to the horizon, one toward the upper left and one toward
the upper right, each ending at a small outbuilding."}

Why two detectors, three thousand kilometers apart? Because a single one cannot
tell a gravitational wave from a passing truck. A real signal has to appear at
both sites within the light-travel time between them — about 10 milliseconds —
with consistent amplitude and shape. Anything local fails that test immediately.

### GW150914

On **14 September 2015** both LIGO detectors saw a signal — first at Livingston,
Louisiana, and then, 7 milliseconds later, at Hanford, Washington. The delay
between the two sites is itself information: it constrains where on the sky the
source was.

Matching the signal against solutions of Einstein's equations identified it as
the merger of two stellar-mass black holes, of about $36\,M_\odot$ and
$29\,M_\odot$. The black hole left behind was about $62\,M_\odot$.

Add those up. $36 + 29 = 65$, and the remnant is 62. **Three solar masses were
converted into energy** and radiated away as gravitational waves, in a fraction
of a second.

![The GW150914 detection. The top row is the strain actually measured at each
site, with Hanford's trace overlaid on Livingston's at the right to show how
well they agree. The second row compares the measurement against a waveform
computed from general relativity for two merging black holes — the theory curve
was not fitted to the data by adjusting the physics, it was *predicted* from it.
The third row is what is left over after subtracting the model, which is noise
and nothing more. The bottom row shows frequency against time: the signal
sweeps upward as the two holes spiral closer and faster, which is the
"chirp." Figure by
[Rothwild](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LIGO_measurement_of_gravitational_waves_multilang.svg),
used under [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/) and
modified to show only the English labels.](gw150914-strain.png){#fig-gw150914
width="100%"
fig-alt="An eight-panel scientific figure in two columns headed Hanford,
Washington and Livingston, Louisiana. The top three rows are line plots of
strain against time: a jagged trace, then a smoother trace with a shaded
uncertainty band around a matching model curve, then a flat noisy residual. The
bottom row shows two dark spectrograms in which a bright yellow-green streak
curves upward toward higher frequency at the right-hand end."}

Look at the second row of @fig-gw150914 for a moment. The smooth curve is not a
fit to the data — it is a solution of Einstein's equations for two black holes
falling together, computed independently. The agreement between that curve and
the measurement is the actual result.

### Pulsar timing arrays

LIGO is sensitive to waves with periods of milliseconds — the frequencies that
stellar-mass black holes merge at. Supermassive black holes, being millions of
times heavier, orbit and merge far more slowly, and radiate at periods of years.
No instrument on Earth is big enough for that.

So instead we use the Galaxy. **Pulsar timing arrays** exploit the fact that
millisecond pulsars are extraordinarily regular clocks. A gravitational wave
passing between us and a pulsar changes the distance the pulses have to travel,
which shifts their arrival times by nanoseconds. Watch enough pulsars across the
sky for long enough and the correlated pattern of those shifts reveals waves
with periods of years.

A third band is coming: **LISA**, a space-based interferometer with arms
millions of kilometers long, originally a joint ESA/NASA mission and now
ESA-led. It will cover the frequencies between the other two.

::::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-waves}

**Exercise 5.11.** GW150914's measured strain was about
$h = 5 \times 10^{-22}$, and LIGO's arms are $4\ \mathrm{km}$ long.

(a) What was the change in arm length?
(b) Compare it with the size of a proton, about $10^{-13}\ \mathrm{cm}$.

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(a)** From @eq-strain, $\Delta x = h\, x$. The strain is a pure number, so
$\Delta x$ inherits the units of $x$ — a length, which is what a change in arm
length had better be. Converting the arm length first:

$$
x = 4\ \mathrm{km} \times \frac{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}
  = 4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm},
$$

$$
\Delta x = (5 \times 10^{-22})(4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm})
         = \boxed{2 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{cm}}.
$$

**(b)**

$$
\frac{\Delta x}{r_p} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{cm}}
                            {10^{-13}\ \mathrm{cm}}
                     = 2 \times 10^{-3},
$$

a pure number, as a ratio of two lengths must be. So the mirrors moved by about
**two thousandths of the width of a proton**, and that displacement was measured
across a 4 km baseline. This is the number that should make the experiment seem
impossible.
::::

**Exercise 5.12.** GW150914 radiated about $3\,M_\odot$ of energy in roughly
20 milliseconds.

(a) How much energy was that, in erg?
(b) What was the average power, in $\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$? Compare it with the
    luminosity of the Sun, $L_\odot = 3.83 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$.

:::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
Part (a) is $E = mc^2$ and nothing more. For part (b), remember that power is
just energy divided by time.

The answers are $5.4 \times 10^{54}\ \mathrm{erg}$ and
$2.7 \times 10^{56}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, which is about
$7 \times 10^{22}\,L_\odot$. Hold that second number up against something: it is
comparable to the combined output of every star in the observable universe. For
about twenty milliseconds, one pair of black holes outshone everything, in a
form of radiation that passed straight through the Earth without anyone
noticing.
::::

**Exercise 5.13.** A binary black hole system produces a strain of $10^{-22}$ at
Earth. If an identical system were ten times further away, what strain would it
produce? *(Strain falls off as $1/d$, not as $1/d^2$.)*

*(No solution given. But it is worth asking yourself why the answer is not
$10^{-24}$, and what it implies about how much more volume of the universe each
improvement in detector sensitivity opens up.)*

:::::

## Loose ends worth knowing

Four things that follow from general relativity and that you should have heard
of, even though we are not going to develop them here.

**Black holes have no hair.** A black hole is completely described by just three
numbers: mass, angular momentum, and electric charge. Nothing else survives.
There is no measurement that tells you whether it formed from hydrogen or
helium, from a star or from a filing cabinet. You met this in
[lecture 2](../spinning-bhs-and-tidal/index.qmd); it is worth knowing that it is
a theorem in general relativity and not merely an observation.

**Hawking radiation.** Black holes are not entirely black. Quantum effects near
the horizon cause them to radiate very faintly, and therefore to evaporate over
time. This is a genuinely important idea theoretically — it is where general
relativity and quantum mechanics collide most productively — but for any
astrophysical black hole the effect is so slow as to be irrelevant. Interesting,
probably not important for anything you will observe.

**The universe must expand or contract.** Einstein's equations applied to the
universe as a whole do not admit a static solution. This bothered Einstein
enough that he added a term to prevent it. Then Hubble showed the universe is
expanding. We will come back to this.

**We have pictures now.** The Event Horizon Telescope combines radio telescopes
across the Earth into an instrument effectively the size of the planet, and has
produced direct images of the shadows of the black holes in M87 and at the
center of our own Galaxy. That shadow's size is set by the photon sphere.


## Summary

- **Curvature has a number**: $r_S/R$, a pure ratio. It is 1 at the horizon,
  goes to 0 far away, and tells you how large a correction general relativity is
  about to make.
- Because everything is written in units of $r_S$, **the mass usually cancels**.
  Strong gravity looks the same around a stellar-mass and a supermassive black
  hole; only the scale changes.
- **Gravitational redshift**: $\lambda = \lambda_0/\sqrt{1 - r_S/r}$. Light
  climbing out of a well loses energy, so its wavelength grows — and it still
  arrives at $c$. Measured on white dwarfs, and on S0-2 at the Galactic center.
- **Gravitational time dilation carries the identical factor**,
  $\Delta\tau = \Delta t\sqrt{1 - r_S/R}$. That is not a coincidence: a wave's
  frequency *is* a clock.
- The derivation runs through **an accelerating ship**, where the clock at the
  back genuinely runs slow and both observers agree it does. Acceleration breaks
  the symmetry that special relativity leaves intact, and the equivalence
  principle turns that into a statement about gravity.
- At the horizon the factor goes to zero: from far away an infalling object
  **never** arrives, fading and reddening forever. By its own clock it crosses
  in finite time and notices nothing. Both accounts are correct.
- **Gravitational waves** are ripples in curvature traveling at $c$, detected by
  LIGO in 2015 at a strain of $5\times10^{-22}$ — a mirror displacement of about
  two thousandths of a proton — and now pursued at other frequencies by pulsar
  timing arrays and, soon, LISA.
- And **the singularity is not a prediction, it is a limit.** Infinite density is
  what a theory says when it has been pushed past its own validity. The horizon
  is real physics; the center is a signpost saying quantum gravity is needed and
  does not yet exist.
